title: Weapons of mass decentralization - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: Argues that the Bronze Age empires never re-formed after c.1200 BC because iron, unlike tin-dependent bronze, could be smelted locally and democratized violence, producing fragmentation, more battles and shorter reigns. Frames military tech by who gets access, and warns that drones (and possibly AI) could similarly erode today's concentrated superpower dominance.

insights.claim: The distribution of access to weapons technology, not just weapon quality, determines whether large centralized empires or fragmented small polities prevail.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Lens for assessing whether a new military/tech platform favors incumbents (concentration) or challengers (fragmentation).
insights.quote: Since iron could be smelted locally, previously peripheral communities could arm themselves with weapons that were, for practical purposes, comparable to the weapons of the elite in the empire’s core.
insights.locator: The blooming of iron / Abundance mindset

insights.claim: Military technologies shift power along two separate axes: the offense-defense balance (e.g. castles) and who can access weaponry (e.g. iron).
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Two-axis framework for classifying defense tech's geopolitical impact.
insights.quote: Some technologies, like castles, change the offense-defense bias – whether it is easier to attack or defend. Others, like iron, change who has access to weaponry.
insights.locator: The iron revolution and its consequences

insights.claim: The real puzzle of the Bronze Age collapse is not why empires fell around 1200 BC but why no comparable empires re-formed for centuries afterwards; catastrophes alone usually cause upheaval without permanently ending civilizations.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Shocks matter less than whether the structural conditions for re-consolidation persist.
insights.quote: The question is not why the Bronze Age empires fell, but why, after they fell, nothing like them returned for centuries.
insights.locator: The Bronze Age collapse – as this

insights.claim: Iron is not a superior material to bronze: good bronze is harder, more predictable, and recyclable thanks to its lower melting point; iron won because of abundance and local availability.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Disruptive technologies can win on cost and accessibility rather than performance—classic low-end disruption.
insights.quote: Iron is different: it is not a better material than bronze. Good bronze is both harder than iron and more predictable.
insights.locator: The advantage of the previous technological leap

insights.claim: Bronze-age imperial power rested on control of scarce tin, which came from a few distant deposits (Afghanistan, France, Iberia, Cornwall), making bronze weapons expensive and concentrated among elites.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Control over a scarce critical input converts directly into geopolitical dominance—relevant to today's critical-mineral chokepoints.
insights.quote: Bronze entrenched this advantage due to a single geological fact: while copper had been somewhat rare, the tin required to transform it into bronze was even rarer.
insights.locator: Copper had come with a growth

insights.claim: Tin traded over very long distances: Cornish tin identified by trace indium appears in shipwrecks near Israel and southern France, and Mari's tin came 500+ miles from Elam, itself ~1,000 miles from Afghan mines.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Ancient precedent for globalized critical-material supply chains vulnerable to disruption.
insights.quote: Texts from the eighteenth century BC record that Mari’s tin traveled over five hundred miles from a kingdom called Elam, which was itself another thousand miles from the Afghan mines that were its likely source.
insights.locator: The city-state of Mari in

insights.claim: Large empires held an edge not only in acquiring bronze but in reliably securing trade links, stockpiling, and replacing losses—sustained state capacity smaller forces lacked.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Scale advantages come from logistics and stockpiles, not just access—relevant to munitions/industrial-base debates.
insights.quote: It was easier for them to obtain supplies, secure trade links, create stockpiles and replace losses.
insights.locator: This had a profound political consequence

insights.claim: Disruption of tin trade routes is listed among candidate causes of the Bronze Age collapse alongside droughts, Sea Peoples raids and internal revolts.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Supply-route disruption for a concentrated input can be a systemic trigger.
insights.locator: The resulting power vacuum set the stage

insights.claim: Iron ore is abundant (iron is the fourth most abundant element in Earth's crust) and easily identified on the surface; Danish Iron Age artifacts used local bog iron smelted with local charcoal.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Abundant inputs collapse incumbents' moat built on scarce-resource control.
insights.quote: One analysis of Iron Age artifacts in Denmark found that the iron was derived from ‘bog iron’ ores that were abundant in local wetlands, smelted with charcoal from local forests.
insights.locator: Transporting tin required a trader

insights.claim: After iron's spread, no early Iron Age empire matched Bronze Age predecessors; the Hittite vacuum was filled by a patchwork of smaller states for centuries.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Cheap force-multipliers tend to produce fragmented multipolar orders rather than new hegemons.
insights.quote: There are no early Iron Age empires as large as their Bronze Age predecessors.
insights.locator: The end of empire

insights.claim: The author's battle-database study finds a sharp rise in battles in the century after a region adopted iron versus the century before, though causation and sample completeness are debated.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Democratized weapons access correlates with more frequent conflict—higher baseline geopolitical risk.
insights.quote: My study based on these databases finds a sharp rise in the number of battles in the century after regions adopted iron compared with the one before.
insights.locator: Databases of battles, made with evidence

insights.claim: Average reign length across Assyria, Babylon and Athens fell 29% after iron adoption, and Babylon saw almost twice as many kings, indicating greater political instability.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Regime turnover rises when coercive power diffuses—proxy for political risk premia.
insights.quote: The average length of reigns across the sample of Assyria, Babylon, and Athens taken together falls 29 percent, and Babylon sees almost twice the number of kings
insights.locator: Ancient records allow us to build

insights.claim: Skeletal remains from the Middle East show more signs of violence in the Late Bronze and Iron Ages than in the Middle Bronze Age.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Physical evidence supports a link between weapons diffusion and violence.
insights.locator: The archaeological record allows us

insights.claim: Ancient writers (Hesiod, Herodotus, Lucretius) associated iron with strife and saw it as equalizing war; the Philistines reportedly tried to restrict access to smiths to prevent iron weapon-making.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Incumbents historically try to regulate access to democratizing tech—an early export-control analogue.
insights.quote: iron made ‘the odds of war equal as they had not been before’
insights.locator: The effects of iron were so stark

insights.claim: Firearms strengthened states while scarce and expensive, but once they became cheap in the 19th-20th centuries they shifted power to peripheral soldiers and rebels; castles empowered barons until gunpowder made walls obsolete.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: New weapon tech is centralizing early and decentralizing as it commoditizes—timing matters.
insights.quote: Gunpowder led to firearms, which strengthened states while they were new, scarce, and expensive, but then became cheap and easily accessible in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries
insights.locator: The iron revolution and its consequences

insights.claim: Nuclear weapons raise the cost of invasion so much that achieving nuclear status can be a powerful equalizer for small states.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Nuclear proliferation incentives persist for smaller states seeking deterrence.
insights.quote: for a small state, achieving nuclear status can be a powerful equalizer
insights.locator: History has seen the ebb and flow

insights.claim: Copper then bronze adoption drove political consolidation: more fortified settlements, greater grave-goods inequality, and specialized smelting sites up to sixty miles from mines, preceding Hittite and Egyptian imperial expansion.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Centralizing technologies coincide with rising inequality and consolidation.
insights.quote: These military successes would not have been possible without bronze.
insights.locator: The spread of bronze preceded a wave

insights.claim: The Iron Age's decentralized political environment gave rise to Greek democracy, Phoenician commerce and writing, and the Abrahamic religions.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Periods of fragmentation can be institutionally generative despite instability.
insights.quote: Greek democracy, Phoenician commerce and writing, and the Abrahamic religions all developed within the new political environment of the Iron Age.
insights.locator: Iron and its consequences laid

insights.claim: Drones are the modern iron: reportedly responsible for up to 80% of recent casualties in the Russia–Ukraine war as of 2026, with a few-hundred-dollar drone able to threaten tanks, artillery and command posts.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Cheap drones erode the value of expensive legacy platforms—bullish low-cost drone makers, bearish exquisite-platform moats.
insights.quote: A drone costing just a few hundred dollars can threaten a tank, artillery gun, or command post worth many times more.
insights.locator: The iron revolution and its consequences

insights.claim: Drone combat lowers war's cost of entry and could make it easier for small guerrilla groups to challenge dominant powers.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Expect more non-state and small-state disruption; higher tail geopolitical risk.
insights.quote: Drone combat has lowered war’s cost of entry and could make it easier for small guerrilla groups to challenge dominant powers.
insights.locator: The iron revolution and its consequences

insights.claim: AI is ambiguous: broadly accessible to individuals, but providers can cut off access, centralizing power like Bronze Age kings controlling tin stores.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: AI providers' gatekeeping power is a strategic chokepoint, with policy and regulatory implications.
insights.quote: Access can be cut off, centralizing the use of AI in the hands of the companies that own it and whomever they choose to allow access
insights.locator: Another parallel can perhaps be seen in AI

insights.claim: Access to violence is currently exceptionally concentrated, letting superpowers reign largely unchallenged, but evolving military technology may usher in a new age of upheaval.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Structural case for a more fragmented, volatile geopolitical order and higher defense spending.
insights.quote: But as military technology evolves, another age of upheaval may be approaching.
insights.locator: Today, we live in an era
